title: Rongbin Han on the Internet Writers Making China Great Again - The Wire China
gist: University of Georgia professor Rongbin Han argues the Chinese Party-state gains legitimacy not by suppressing online expression but by licensing citizens to co-author nationalist fantasy — alt-history web novels in which time travelers industrialize China early and beat the West — inside boundaries set by censorship, platform editor micromanagement and co-option into Party writing bodies. His framework replaces the 'control-resistance' binary with participatory authoritarianism, and his stated fear is Huxley's Brave New World rather than Orwell's 1984.

insights.claim: The Chinese Party-state adds to regime legitimacy over the long run by allowing citizens to participate in constructing the popular imagination of national greatness rather than dictating it, because participation produces narratives the population will actually accept and embrace.
insights.speaker: Ella Apostoaie
insights.so_what: Analysts modeling Chinese political risk on the assumption that repression alone sustains the regime will systematically under-forecast its durability and its capacity to absorb economic disappointment.
insights.quote: But when the Party says, “You write the novels, imagine whatever you want to imagine, with me setting the bottom line,” it actually activates popular participation in the process.
insights.locator: I argue that the Party, by allowing people to participate

insights.claim: Online political expression in China is not particularly threatening to the ruling party because the internet produces polarization — critics and defenders of the government whose opinions cancel each other out.
insights.speaker: Ella Apostoaie
insights.so_what: Explains why Beijing tolerates a noisy internet: online criticism is a pressure release rather than a regime-change vector, so viral dissent episodes are poor signals of instability.
insights.quote: Those opinions will ultimately cancel each other out, so they are not really threatening the regime or the Party.
insights.locator: In my first book, I found that political expression

insights.claim: Chinese political apathy is widespread and official media messaging often backfires, with a large share of the public actively alert to anything the Party tries to implant in them — which is precisely why outsourcing narrative production to commercial writers works better than direct propaganda.
insights.speaker: Ella Apostoaie
insights.so_what: Diminishing returns on state propaganda mean influence increasingly flows through commercial platforms and creators — the leverage point for anyone assessing Chinese information environment or platform regulation.
insights.locator: There is pretty widespread political apathy in China

insights.claim: The dominant 'control-resistance paradigm' for analyzing the Chinese internet — a tool either for state control or citizen resistance — captures only part of reality and misses the rich, dynamic non-political experience that carries political implications.
insights.speaker: Ella Apostoaie
insights.so_what: A better analytical lens for China tech policy: entertainment and commerce platforms are where legitimacy is manufactured, so regulation of gaming, literature and short video is political infrastructure, not consumer policy.
insights.locator: I call this a control-resistance paradigm

insights.claim: The more plausible dystopian endpoint for China is not Orwell's 1984 but Aldous Huxley's Brave New World, in which people amuse themselves to death — a state not yet reached.
insights.speaker: Ella Apostoaie
insights.so_what: Reframes the Chinese consumer internet as the primary instrument of political stability, implying entertainment consumption trends are a legitimacy indicator worth tracking.
insights.quote: the most fearful outcome for me is actually Aldous Huxley’s Brave New World, where people amuse themselves to death
insights.locator: Maybe we shouldn’t use George Orwell’s 1984 metaphor

themes.theme: How censorship actually works in long-form web fiction

insights.claim: Censorship of book-length internet literature in China operates preemptively through platform-assigned editors who micromanage plotlines and warn writers away from directions they see developing, rather than through after-the-fact deletion of posts.
insights.speaker: Ella Apostoaie
insights.so_what: Content risk in Chinese platform businesses is embedded in editorial headcount and workflow, not just takedown tooling — a structural cost and a source of sudden campaign-driven supply shocks in content pipelines.
insights.locator: Internet literature is produced daily for people to consume daily

insights.claim: Chinese internet fiction covers a historical span from the first dynasty to the reform era but almost never the years between 1949 and 1978, since the Maoist era, the Cultural Revolution and the Great Famine are entirely off the table for anyone writing for a living.
insights.speaker: Ella Apostoaie
insights.so_what: A measurable, testable censorship footprint: the absence of an entire three-decade setting demonstrates how economic incentives make writers self-police far more efficiently than enforcement could.
insights.quote: There’s a joke on the internet about how the government of China is actually the Time and Space Administration.
insights.locator: There’s a joke on the internet about how the government

insights.claim: Writing about communism is a censorship trap even when it flatters official history: the novel Red Dawn, in which a modern man travels to 1905 and copies the Communist Party's own ideology, tactics, mobilization and land reform, was censored by the Party despite remaining widely discussed.
insights.speaker: Ella Apostoaie
insights.so_what: Compliance in China is not reducible to ideological alignment — even pro-regime content is censorable, which makes content-platform risk fundamentally unhedgeable by editorial stance alone.
insights.locator: One of them is called Red Dawn

insights.claim: Religious themes are effectively taboo in Chinese web fiction: one writer's editor blocked a plot about a religion splitting into moderate and extreme factions in an entirely alternate universe because readers would think of Islam.
insights.speaker: Ella Apostoaie
insights.so_what: Illustrates how far Chinese content restriction extends into pure fiction by analogy — a wider risk surface than keyword lists imply for any AI or media firm operating in China.
insights.locator: Religion is a taboo topic in some senses

insights.claim: The Party regulates publishing platforms through a detailed grading system in which platforms gain or lose points depending on whether they meet social-responsibility goals for the writing they host.
insights.speaker: Ella Apostoaie
insights.so_what: A points-scored regulatory regime creates quantifiable, non-transparent compliance risk for Chinese content platforms — worth pricing into any exposure to Chinese digital publishing.
insights.locator: The Party issues regulations about how publishing platforms

insights.claim: Beyond censorship the Party co-opts writers directly: many internet writers now belong to the Party-run China Writers Association and its Internet Literature Committee, and some successful writers have become members of Chinese People's Political Consultative Conferences at various levels.
insights.speaker: Ella Apostoaie
insights.so_what: Institutional co-option of top creators means the most commercially successful Chinese content producers are structurally aligned with state objectives — relevant to assessing any Chinese cultural export.
insights.locator: The Party also co-opts people

insights.claim: The Party mainly promotes rather than bans, using numerous literary awards that go to works it deems to have 'positive energy' — for example The Industrial Tycoon by Qicheng, whose author received a number of government awards.
insights.speaker: Ella Apostoaie
insights.so_what: Positive incentives, not just prohibitions, shape Chinese content markets — meaning state preference is legible in award lists and can be used to forecast which genres get commercial runway.
insights.locator: Mostly, the Party promotes what it likes

insights.claim: Chinese web novels are subject to the attention economy and must produce what the market wants, which is why Han nationalist premises dominate — most authors and readers are Han Chinese and gravitate to fixing history before Manchu Qing or Mongol Yuan rule.
insights.speaker: Ella Apostoaie
insights.so_what: Nationalist sentiment in China is commercially demand-driven, not merely state-supplied, so it will not soften just because official messaging does.
insights.quote: Web novels are subject to the attention economy; you need to produce what the market wants.
insights.locator: The Ming Dynasty is unique in a number of ways

insights.claim: The Ming dynasty is the majority setting for Chinese alt-history time-travel fiction because it coincides with the West beginning to explore and industrialize, making it the perceived critical juncture where China fell behind.
insights.speaker: Ella Apostoaie
insights.so_what: Reveals the popular Chinese diagnosis of national decline as a technology and industrialization failure — the cultural substrate beneath state tech self-sufficiency policy.
insights.locator: Also, a lot of works discuss why China fell behind

insights.claim: The 'Industrial Party' strand of Chinese online thought, exemplified by the collectively written Morning Star of Lingao (over 9 million characters and still ongoing), holds that the only strategy China should pursue is industrialization and further industrialization.
insights.speaker: Ella Apostoaie
insights.so_what: A grassroots constituency for manufacturing-first policy explains the political durability of China's industrial subsidy programs even when returns on capital are poor.
insights.quote: the only kind of strategy China should pursue is industrialization and further industrialization
insights.locator: This work represents the “Industrial Party,”

insights.claim: The state-awarded novel The Industrial Tycoon has its protagonist travel to 1979, build an industrial empire by exploiting the Soviet collapse to acquire Soviet technical knowledge, and concludes with China's first nuclear-powered aircraft carrier visiting the port of New York.
insights.speaker: Ella Apostoaie
insights.so_what: Naval parity with the United States is not just a military program but an officially rewarded popular aspiration — a signal that Chinese defense build-out has broad domestic demand behind it.
insights.locator: One of those works, included in my study

themes.theme: What the genre reveals about Chinese confidence

insights.claim: Contemporary Chinese alt-history fiction differs from late Qing and early Republican science fiction in its temporal direction: the earlier era, suffering national humiliation, could only imagine a great future, while today's writers assume China is already doing well and its rise is imminent, so the only unfinished business is the past.
insights.speaker: Ella Apostoaie
insights.so_what: A direct read on Chinese popular sentiment: confidence about trajectory rather than anxiety, which argues against Western assumptions that economic slowdown quickly translates into domestic political crisis.
insights.quote: They see China doing very well right now, and that China’s rise is imminent. The only thing they want to do is go back into history and make up for historical sorrows.
insights.locator: Why? They see China doing very well right now

insights.claim: Alt-history internet fiction in China is not necessarily anti-government, because everything is produced, shared and consumed inside the Great Firewall where overtly anti-Party content would be censored out of existence.
insights.speaker: Ella Apostoaie
insights.so_what: Any inference about Chinese public opinion drawn from domestically visible online content is systematically bounded — a sampling constraint to apply when reading Chinese sentiment data.
insights.locator: These writings are produced and shared and consumed within the Great Firewall

insights.claim: Foreign visitors filming China for YouTube and TikTok — praising clean cities, fast internet, impressive infrastructure, high-speed trains and affordable groceries — perform soft-power work for the Chinese government at zero cost to Beijing.
insights.speaker: Ella Apostoaie
insights.so_what: China's international image is increasingly shaped by third-party creator content rather than state media, which makes travel reopening and visa liberalization cheap, high-return influence policy.
insights.quote: Tourists just come in, take a look, and then talk about everything they see there.
insights.locator: When foreigners go to China and they film things

insights.claim: The Chinese internet is neither borderless nor fully walled off: martial arts and mystical fiction from Chinese platforms is being translated into English for foreign audiences even as political content stays inside.
insights.speaker: Ella Apostoaie
insights.so_what: Chinese content IP has a proven export channel in genre fiction — a niche but real path for Chinese cultural exports that bypasses political friction.
insights.locator: There are a bunch of Chinese novels, not the “Make China Great Again”-type

insights.claim: The state does not have to write the narrative it prefers: commercial writers seeking popularity spread it themselves, connecting the Party to the people more organically than Party propaganda ever could.
insights.speaker: Ella Apostoaie
insights.so_what: The lowest-cost, highest-efficacy propaganda model in China is market-mediated, implying Beijing will keep expanding rather than shrinking commercial creative sectors it can lightly steer.
insights.locator: The party does carefully manage everything, but who writes these online stories?
